lesson.title: The Species That Holds the Arch Together: Keystone Species
lesson.summary: A keystone species is a species whose impact on its community is far larger than its abundance alone would suggest, so that removing it can cause the whole community structure to collapse or radically change.
lesson.body:
An arch made of stone stays standing because of one particular stone at the very top, the keystone, that holds the whole curved structure together, even though it is just one stone among many. Ecologists borrow this image for a keystone species: a species whose effect on the structure and diversity of its community is disproportionately large compared to how abundant or how much biomass it actually represents. Remove a keystone species and, unlike removing most other species, the whole community can shift dramatically, sometimes collapsing into a much simpler, less diverse state.

The term itself was coined by the ecologist Robert Paine, based on field experiments he ran in the late 1960s on the rocky intertidal shores of the Pacific coast of Washington state. Paine studied a predatory sea star, Pisaster ochraceus, which fed on mussels growing on the rocks. When he experimentally removed the sea stars from study plots, the mussels, freed from their main predator, multiplied and spread rapidly, crowding out and eliminating most of the other species, various algae, barnacles, and smaller invertebrates, that had previously coexisted in that space. The number of species in the plots fell sharply. Sea stars were not the most abundant organism in the community, but their predation on mussels, an interaction that also connects back to the ideas of predation and competition covered earlier in this unit, was what kept mussels from taking over and squeezing everything else out.

A second, especially well known keystone species example comes from the kelp forests of the Pacific coast, involving sea otters. Sea otters prey heavily on sea urchins, which in turn graze on kelp, a large, fast growing marine algae that forms dense underwater forests supporting many other species. Research on this system, notably by the ecologists James Estes and John Palmisano in the 1970s, found that in areas where sea otters were present, urchin populations stayed low and kelp forests flourished. In areas where otters had been eliminated by hunting, urchin populations exploded, and their intense grazing could strip an area of kelp almost entirely, leaving behind what ecologists call an urchin barren, a rocky seafloor with little life compared to a thriving kelp forest. The otters were not the most numerous species in the system, but their predation on urchins made the difference between a rich kelp forest ecosystem and a barren one.

What both of these cases show is that a species' ecological importance cannot be judged just by how common it is. A keystone species can be relatively rare and still exert control over an entire community's structure, through the chain of interactions it sets off. That chain of effects, rippling outward from one species' influence through multiple levels of a food web, is exactly what the next chapter, on trophic cascades, examines in more detail.
